We need to propose a retrosynthesis route with 1 reaction for target SMILES: [CH2:1]=[C:2]([c:3]1[cH:4][cH:5][cH:6][cH:7][cH:8]1)[C@@H:9]1[CH2:10][CH2:11][CH2:12][C@@:13]1([OH:14])[C:15]([F:16])([F:17])[F:18]

Let's decode: It's a bicyclic? Actually it's a cyclopentanol fused? Let's interpret: There's an exocyclic alkene attached to a phenyl ring and to a cyclopentane bearing CF3 and OH? Wait: The SMILES: CH2=C( c1ccccc1 )C@@H1CCCC1O? plus CF3 attached to carbon 15? Actually after the cyclopentane, there is [C:15]([F:16])([F:17])[F:18] attached to the same carbon as OH? Let's parse: [C@@H:9]1[CH2:10][CH2:11][CH2:12][C@@:13]1([OH:14])[C:15]([F:16])([F:17])[F:18]

So carbon 9 is chiral attached to ring (C1...). The ring is a cyclobutane? Actually numbering: C9 is attached to CH2= C(Ph) group and to a 5-membered ring: C9-CH2-CH2-CH2-C13 (closing to C9). C13 has OH and also attached to CF3 carbon (C15). So it's a bicyclic? Actually it's a cyclopentanol with CF3 substituent.

The retrosynthetic step is a carbonyl-ene reaction (forward). So retrosynthesis: break the C-O bond (hydroxyl) to a carbonyl (ketone) and break C=C to form alkene. So the precursor would be a ketone (probably a cyclopentanone with CF3) and an alkene (maybe an allylic hydrogen). In carbonyl-ene, the product has new C-C bond between alkene carbon and carbonyl carbon, forming a new C-O (hydroxyl) at the allylic position. So reverse: we need to disconnect the C-C bond formed between the alkene carbon (the exocyclic alkene carbon) and the carbonyl carbon (which becomes the carbon bearing OH). So the precursor would be a cyclopentanone with CF3 at carbon adjacent to carbonyl? Let's think: In product, carbon 13 (bearing OH) is attached to CF3 carbon (C15). In carbonyl-ene, the carbonyl carbon becomes the carbon bearing OH after reaction (the ene product). So the carbonyl carbon in precursor is C13 (the carbon bearing OH in product). So precursor is a cyclopentanone (C13 carbonyl) with CF3 attached to same carbon? Actually carbonyl carbon cannot have CF3 attached; carbonyl carbon is C=O, attached to two groups: one is the ring (C9) and the other is CF3? That would be a trifluoroacetyl? Not typical. Wait maybe the CF3 is attached to adjacent carbon (C15) which is attached to C13 after reaction? In product, C13 is attached to OH and to C15 (CF3). In precursor, C13 is carbonyl carbon attached to C15 (CF3) and to C9 (ring). So it's a ketone: C13=O, attached to C9 and CF3 carbon (C15). So precursor is a cyclopentanone with a CF3 substituent at carbonyl carbon (i.e., a trifluoroacetyl cyclopentane?). Actually that would be a trifluoromethyl ketone: O=C(C(F)(F)F)C1CCCC1? plus the exocyclic alkene attached to C9? Wait C9 is attached to alkene carbon (C2) and to ring. In precursor, C9 is attached to carbonyl carbon (C13) and to alkene? The carbonyl-ene forms a new C-C bond between alkene carbon (C2) and carbonyl carbon (C13). So in precursor, C9 is attached to carbonyl carbon (C13) and to alkene carbon (C2) is not yet formed? Actually the alkene is separate: we have an alkene (CH2= C(Ph)-) that will undergo ene with the carbonyl. The allylic hydrogen is on the alkene? In carbonyl-ene, the alkene provides an allylic hydrogen that transfers to carbonyl oxygen, forming OH. So the alkene must have an allylic hydrogen adjacent to the double bond. In our product, the OH is on C13 (former carbonyl). The allylic hydrogen came from the alkene's allylic position (the CH2 of the exocyclic alkene? The alkene is CH2=C(Ph)- attached to C9. The allylic hydrogen is on the CH2 (C1) which becomes the OH? Actually the CH2 becomes OH after transfer? In product, the OH is on C13, not on the alkene. So the hydrogen transferred from the alkene's allylic position (the CH2) to the carbonyl oxygen, generating OH on carbonyl carbon. So the precursor alkene must have a CH2 adjacent to the double bond (allylic). In our product, the CH2 is now part of the double bond (exocyclic). So the precursor would be a saturated alkane? Wait.

Simplify: Use known carbonyl-ene retrosynthesis: product is allylic alcohol; precursor is carbonyl + alkene. So we can propose that the target can be derived from a ketone (CF3-substituted cyclopentanone) and an alkene (styrene derivative) via carbonyl-ene. So the retrosynthetic step: break the C-O bond to carbonyl, break the C-C bond between C9 and C2 to separate alkene.

Thus the precursor set: 1) CF3-substituted cyclopentanone (structure: O=C(C(F)(F)F)C1CCCC1) attached to C9? Actually the carbonyl carbon is attached to C9 (part of ring) and CF3. That's O=C(C(F)(F)F)C1CCCC1 (where the carbonyl carbon is part of the ring? Wait C1CCCC1 includes carbonyl carbon? The carbonyl carbon is part of the ring? In cyclopentanone, carbonyl carbon is part of the ring. So O=C(C(F)(F)F)C1CCCC1 would be a cyclopentanone with CF3 attached to carbonyl carbon (exocyclic). That's plausible.

2) Alkene: CH2= C(Ph)- (i.e., styrene). Actually the alkene is CH2=C(Ph)- attached to C9 in product. In precursor, the alkene is separate: CH2= C(Ph)- (styrene). The carbon attached to C9 is the carbon of the double bond that will form bond to carbonyl carbon. So the alkene is styrene (C= Cc1ccccc1). The double bond carbon attached to the carbonyl carbon is the internal carbon (C). So the alkene is CH2= C(Ph)- (i.e., 1-phenyl-ethylene). That's styrene.

Thus retrosynthesis: target -> via carbonyl-ene -> precursors: (a) 2,2,2-trifluoro-1-cyclopentanone (or 2,2,2-trifluoro-cyclopentanone) and (b) styrene.

We need to find a template ID for carbonyl-ene reaction. Let's search for templates with functional groups broken: ketones, C-C double bonds; formed: aliphatic hydroxyls, five-membered rings. Use correct functional group names: "ketones", "C-C double bonds" broken; formed: "aliphatic hydroxyls", "five-membered rings". Also bonds broken: "C=O", "C=C". bonds formed: "C-C". Let's try search again with correct names.
